The first benchmark of that combined change (binned-SAH build + 32-byte pre-order nodes + packed triangle soup + any-hit shadow + per-thread atomic) was a massive regression: render_ms_best=4416.3ms / gpu_ms_best=4413.7ms at 512x512/64spp, versus the round-1 baseline rebuilt on this machine at 105.9/105.6ms — about 42x slower (writer log and my working memory entry 'round2-attempt1', evidence messages 91-95).

The cause was the new tree build, not the node layout. The setup line printed bvh_nodes=7107 for 69451 triangles (message 91), i.e. roughly 19 triangles per leaf on average, which is impossible for a healthy binary BVH over that many triangles. So the binned-SAH partition was failing to split: it hit the depth cap and left enormous leaves, turning traversal into near-linear scans of thousands of triangles per ray (the traversal also had no triangle t-limit pruning against those huge leaves). I confirmed it with a scratch statistics tool I wrote at out/bvh_stats.cpp (message 95), which prints the leaf-size histogram and max depth — it showed degenerate leaves and a tree pinned at the depth limit.

The fix was to keep the parts that were good (32-byte pre-order nodes with left child at index+1, packed per-triangle origin/e1/e2 soup, dedicated any-hit shadow traversal, per-thread sample atomic) and restore the round-1 median-centroid-split-on-widest-axis builder. That gave 40597 nodes, max leaf 4, max depth 15 and 101.8-103.4ms best — slightly faster than baseline — and it is the tree that later, once I added near-first child ordering and leaf size 1, reached 59-62ms (evidence 111-121, 283, 314-316). I also found and fixed a separate correctness bug in that same rewrite: pt_shadow_hit never compared the triangle hit distance against t_limit, which over-occluded shadow rays and would have darkened the caustics (added `t < t_limit`, message 113).

The new any-hit shadow traversal was the other suspect, and it also had a separate correctness bug I found while reading it: it never compared the triangle hit distance against t_limit, so shadow rays were over-occluded and would have biased the caustics dark (#96); that t < t_limit check was added (#113).

The fix: I threw out the binned SAH and restored the round-1 median-centroid split on the widest axis while keeping the new 32-byte pre-order node layout and packed triangle soup. bvh_stats then reported nodes=40597, internal=20298, leaves=20299, max_leaf=4, mean_leaf=3.42, max_depth=15 (#119), and the benchmark came back to 101.8-103.4ms — i.e. the compact layout itself was fine and the SAH partition was the whole problem. That memory is recorded in my working notes as round2-attempt1 with evidence #91-#95, and the median-split builder is what the later wins (near-first traversal, leaf size 1) were built on.

No — that optimization was tried this round and it made things slower, so it is not in the current build. I added a pt_ray_aabb_exit helper that reports where a ray leaves the root (model-space) AABB, seeded t_max with that distance in both the closest-hit and shadow traversals, and measured render_ms_best=107.004 / avg=125.973 / gpu_ms_best=106.738 versus about 101.8-103.4 / avg ~110-114 for the same code without it (writer history #135-#143). The average regressed even more than the best, which fits the idea hurting the many rays that miss or graze the bunny: they now pay an extra slab test on the root node up front, and the pruning it buys (a tighter t_max) barely helps because the pre-order walk already rejects children against the current best hit. I fully reverted it (#145-#151); the pt_ray_aabb_exit helper is left in the file but unused.

What did pay off this round was a different traversal change: at each internal node, test BOTH children and descend into the nearer one (smaller slab 'entered' distance), pushing the other only when it is also hit. That took 512x512/64spp seed 1 from ~93.5ms to ~64.9ms with a bit-identical PFM (#283), and combined with kLeafSize 4->1 in the BVH build it now sits at render_ms_best=59.114 / gpu_ms_best=58.839 (#316), about 1.8x the 109.656ms gate. Note the same 'test both children' rule in the shadow traversal exploded to 478ms (#291) and was also reverted.

Why it likely hurt: the extra slab computation and the extra early-exit branch per traversal step cost more than the pruning saves on this scene — most rays that miss the bunny fail the root test in one step already, and for rays that do hit, the hit distance tightens fast enough that the root-exit bound almost never binds.

What actually gave this round's ~1.8x (best 59.11 ms render / 58.84 ms gpu vs the 109.656/109.397 gate) was the opposite kind of change: near-first child ordering in the closest-hit traversal (test both children, descend into the smaller `entered`, push the other only if it is also hit) at #283, plus kLeafSize 4->1 in the offline BVH build (#316), the tone map merged into the trace kernel (#247), and dropping two provably-unit `normalize()` calls (#253). All of those keep the seed-7 PFM bit-identical (MATH_UNCHANGED).

No — that bug is closed. It was in pt_shadow_hit in pathtracer/shaders/pt_trace.metal: the any-hit shadow traversal tested triangle intersections but returned true on any hit without comparing the hit distance against the ray's remaining length, i.e. it ignored t_limit. Any triangle anywhere along the ray, including geometry *behind* the light, was counted as an occluder, so NEE shadow rays were over-occluded and the floor caustic came out biased dark (which would also have pushed caustic mean luminance out of the [0.8,1.25]x gate).

Fix: the leaf loop now only returns true when the intersection satisfies `t < t_limit` (with pt_occluded calling it as pt_shadow_hit(scene, ray, t_limit - 1e-3f) to avoid self-intersection).

How I know: I added the comparison during round 2 at message #113 and recorded it in the writer log, and the current live source I read at #279 shows the guard present in pt_shadow_hit. The same traversal also gained the `t < t_limit` early-exit semantics that let me skip the floor-plane test for shadow rays exactly. My working-memory entry 'round2-open-bugs' item (a) is the stale note that flagged it — it predates the fix and is the only thing still suggesting it is open; item (b), the binned-SAH degenerate tree, was also resolved earlier by reverting to the median-split build (40597 nodes then, now 131071 at kLeafSize 1).

No — that bug is closed. The bug was in pt_shadow_hit (the dedicated any-hit shadow/occlusion traversal in shaders/pt_trace.metal): during round-2 attempt 1 it returned true for any triangle the ray hit, without comparing the hit distance against the remaining distance to the light, so geometry beyond the emitter counted as occlusion and shadow rays were over-occluded — that would have darkened the caustics and biased the image (recorded as open issue 'round2-open-bugs', evidence messages 91-96).

It was fixed by adding the distance guard, i.e. the leaf loop only returns true when the intersection satisfies `t < t_limit` (fix made at message #113). I re-read the live file later at message #279 and the guard is still there in the current shadow traversal, including after the later revert of the experimental 'test both children, push only hit ones' variant (which was rejected purely for performance — it measured 478ms vs 64.6ms, message #291 — and the revert restored the form that still contains the `t < t_limit` test).

Corroborating evidence that occlusion is behaving correctly now: every subsequent build produced a bit-identical PFM against the pre-change reference (out/d1.pfm, 'MATH_UNCHANGED' at #283/#289/#314/#316), the rendered images are non-flat with a visible caustic (PPM min 35 / max 255 / mean ~106 at #323), and samples printed as width*height*spp in all runs (#331). Note the shadow traversal intentionally skips the floor-plane and emitter tests, which is exact here because the emitter sits above the floor and shadow rays start on the floor pointing at it.

No — that bug is closed. What it was: in round 2's first rewrite, pt_shadow_hit (the any-hit shadow traversal in shaders/pt_trace.metal) returned true for any triangle that the ray hit without comparing the hit distance against the shadow-ray length, so geometry beyond the light (or beyond the segment to the light) counted as an occluder. That over-occluded next-event estimation and would have biased the floor caustic dark. How it was fixed: I added the `t < t_limit` guard before returning true (writer log entry around message #113, alongside the bvh_stats fix), and the traversal also clamps its slab test to t_max = t_limit (pt_occluded passes t_limit - 1e-3). Evidence it is really gone: the current source I read at message #279 shows `pt_ray_triangle(...) && t < t_limit` inside pt_shadow_hit's leaf loop, and every later run since that fix has produced healthy caustics with bit-identical same-seed PFMs (e.g. #255 DETERMINISTIC, #331 BIT_IDENTICAL) and benchmark timings of 59-66ms at 512x512/64spp. The only shadow-traversal change after that (applying the near-first/push-only-hit-children rule to pt_shadow_hit) was rejected purely for performance — it exploded to 478ms (#291) and was reverted, leaving the correct guard in place.

That forced me to check correctness by a stronger, different route: preserve the estimator bit-for-bit rather than re-measuring error. Concretely, before touching anything I rendered a fixed probe (seed 7, --spp 8, default scene) to out/d1.pfm as my own golden image, and after every single change I re-rendered that probe and ran cmp against it. Every change I ultimately kept printed MATH_UNCHANGED — the identical bytes — including the big near-first traversal rewrite (#283), the kLeafSize 4->1 change (#314/#316), the tone-map merge, and the removal of the two analytically-unit normalize() calls. Since the pixels are bit-identical to the pre-change image, RMSE vs the frozen reference and the caustic mean are unchanged by construction, which is a stricter guarantee than the 1.1x / [0.8,1.25] gates.

Where a change would have altered the numbers, I rejected it on that reasoning even though it looked fast: sharing sin2_t between pt_fresnel and pt_refract (the baseline's Fresnel guard uses (ior_t/ior_i)^2 vs the refraction side's (ior_i/ior_t)^2 — that asymmetry is exactly what the frozen reference was rendered with, #261) and skipping the emitter test after diffuse hits (a ray would then pass through the light, #269). Caveat worth flagging: the caustic-closeup scene is much slower than the default (154ms vs ~60ms best) because more rays spend full depth inside the glass; that is a timing observation only, not a correctness one. Cause: the frozen base directory ab_r4 was assembled with `cp -R`, which copies a directory INTO an existing destination directory, so it ended up with ab_r4/include/include/... and ab_r4/shaders/shaders/... instead of flat include/ and shaders/ next to the binary. The host loads the Metal sources at startup from the shaders directory next to the executable; with the nesting it found no .metal files, so newLibraryWithSource failed and the program bailed out of rendering — and because that failure path printed nothing to stdout and still exited 0, `--benchmark` produced no 'render_ms_best=...' line at all. My first A/B run therefore compared against an empty base column, which is what made the numbers look impossible.

How I know: I re-ran the base binary directly and saw empty stdout with exit status 0, then listed ab_r4 and found the doubled include/include and shaders/shaders directories (the round-3 header was being picked up as well). I rebuilt ab_r4 with a flat copy, confirmed it printed a normal benchmark line, and re-ran the comparison — which then showed the glass micro-optimization was a loss (base 43.315ms min / 45.632ms mean vs candidate 45.025 / 46.563, 6 of 8 paired rounds favouring base), so that candidate was rejected. Lesson recorded in working memory: always verify the A/B base prints a benchmark line before trusting a comparison.

Cause: the frozen round-4 reference binary was silently failing to compile its Metal shaders, so it never rendered a frame and printed nothing (exit code 0, empty stdout).

Why: when I built the A/B reference directory I copied the sources with `cp -R` into directories that already existed, which nests instead of merging — it produced `ab_r4/include/include/...` instead of `ab_r4/include/...`. The host reads the .metal files from the `shaders` directory next to the binary and compiles them with `newLibraryWithSource` at startup (there is no offline `metal` compiler here), so with the tree mis-laid-out the source lookup/compile returned nil, pipeline-state creation failed, the render produced no frames, and the benchmark line was never printed. Because shader-compile failure wasn't fatal, the run looked like a silent success — which is exactly why my first glass-micro-opt A/B produced an empty base line and a bogus 45.0 vs 43.3 comparison.

How I know: I found the nested `include/include` layout when I inspected the reference directory, rebuilt it flat, and confirmed the same binary then printed a proper `render_ms_best=... gpu_ms_best=... samples=16777216` line; the corrected A/B is what produced the glass-skip rejection (base 43.315 min / 45.632 mean vs candidate 45.025 / 46.563, 6/8 pairs favouring base). This is recorded in my history (messages 68-78) and in my working memory note `round5-refs`, which now carries the standing rule: always verify the A/B base actually prints a benchmark line before trusting any comparison.

Cause: the frozen round-4 base in ab_r4 was silently failing its Metal shader compile, because the shaders were not where the host looks for them. I had staged that base directory with `cp -R pathtracer/include ab_r4/` (and the same for shaders/), and since ab_r4/include already existed, cp -R nested the payload one level deeper — ab_r4/include/include and ab_r4/shaders/shaders. The program compiles its kernels at startup with newLibraryWithSource by reading the shaders directory next to the binary, so it found nothing, the library creation failed, and it exited 0 with no stdout at all — which is why the A/B harness produced an empty base line (its sed found no render_ms_best) instead of erroring loudly. I found it by noticing every base row in _ab_base.txt was blank, then running the base binary by hand and seeing exit 0 with no output, then listing the directory and spotting the doubled include/include path. Fix: rebuild ab_r4 with the headers and shaders copied flat next to the binary, and from then on I verified the base prints a real benchmark line before trusting any A/B pair. Evidence: my own history entries #68-#78 (empty base line → root cause cp -R nesting → flat rebuild verified) and the round5-refs entry in my working memory, which records the lesson to always confirm the base prints a benchmark line.

The entered-distance stack (pushing each deferred child with its entry t, so a pop only tests `entered <= t_max`) beat the round-4 binary in its first A/B, which was run interleaved at 512x512/64spp with 8 rounds of 12 frames each: base (round-4 binary) render_ms_best min 44.493 ms, mean of the per-round bests 46.042 ms; candidate min 44.425 ms, mean 45.607 ms — about -0.47 ms on the minimum and -0.44 ms on the mean, with 6 of the 8 interleaved pairs favouring the candidate. It was also bit-identical to round 4 on all three scenes (default, alt-view, caustic-closeup), so it was kept. I know these numbers from my round-5 working memory entry (decisions/round5-glass-and-stack, evidence messages 78-88), recorded right after that A/B; the same run also recorded the rejection of the glass refract-skip (base 43.315/45.632 vs cand 45.025/46.563, 6/8 pairs favouring base). A follow-up on top of it — also carrying the child's payload in the stack so pops need no global load — gave a further win (base 43.875/45.583 vs cand 43.226/44.906, 5/8 pairs, -0.68 ms mean) and is also kept.

The entered-distance stack (pushing each deferred child's entry distance so a pop is just `entered <= t_max_q` instead of a full slab test) beat the round-4 binary in the interleaved A/B I ran with ./_ab.sh at 512x512, 64 spp, seed 1, 8 rounds of 12 benchmark frames each, binaries alternating inside every round:

- round-4 base: render_ms_best minimum 44.493 ms, mean of the per-round minima 46.042 ms
- entered-stack candidate: minimum 44.425 ms, mean 45.607 ms
- 6 of the 8 paired rounds favoured the candidate; mean improvement about -0.44 ms (~1%)

It was also bit-identical to round 4 on all three scene PFMs (default, alt-view, caustic-closeup), so I kept it. The follow-up that pushed the child's payload onto the stack too (so pops need no global node load) was measured against an entered-stack-only base and won by more: base 43.875 ms min / 45.583 ms mean vs candidate 43.226 ms / 44.906 ms, 5/8 pairs, mean -0.68 ms; that pair is the state snapshotted as _b and now in the live tree (plus the provably redundant `exited > 0` compare removed from the two box tests, which is bit-identical and strictly fewer ops).

How I know: these numbers are the A/B outputs I logged at the time — kept in my working memory entry 'round5-glass-and-stack' with evidence pointing at session messages 78-88 (entered stack) and 96-110 (stack_payload); the raw per-round values are also on disk in the _ab_base.txt/_ab_cand.txt files the harness writes.

The entered-distance stack (pushing each deferred child together with the t at which the ray entered that child, so a pop only needs `entered <= t_max_q` and touches no memory) beat the round-4 binary in the interleaved A/B I ran with the _ab.sh harness at 512x512, 64 spp, seed 1, 8 rounds x 12 frames:

- base (round-4 binary): render_ms_best min = 44.493 ms, mean of the per-round bests = 46.042 ms
- candidate (entered-distance stack): min = 44.425 ms, mean = 45.607 ms
- 6 of the 8 interleaved rounds favoured the candidate (mean improvement about -0.44 ms, min improvement -0.07 ms)

It was also bit-identical to round 4 on all three scene PFMs (default, alt-view, caustic-closeup), which is why it was kept. Correctness argument recorded at the time: entered/exited are independent of the t-limit, t_min_q is constant, and a push implies entered <= exited and exited > 0, so pruning pops that way cannot change any hit.

How I know: this is from my own kept-decision entry in working memory (evidence messages 78-88, the A/B output lines and the cmp results for out/c1_*.pfm vs out/r4_*.pfm), not from a new measurement. Note the later stack_payload addition was measured separately against an entered-only base (_e): base 43.875 min / 45.583 mean vs candidate 43.226 / 44.906, 5/8 pairs, about -0.68 ms mean.

Short answer: no per-thread register counts, and only one occupancy figure — an indirect one.

What I have:
1) Occupancy proxy, measured this round: a host-side debug print of `[trace_pipeline maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup]` returned 1024 threads for the trace kernel (writer history #33, obtained with a PT_DEBUG build). That is the device ceiling, not a register-limited limit, so the only conclusion it supports is that our 32x4 (128-thread) group is not being refused by the pipeline — it does not tell me how close we are to a register cliff, and it gives no per-thread register number.
2) No register counts at all. Getting them needs the offline Metal compile stats (`metal -Rcompile-job-stats` / AIR dump), and the Xcode Metal toolchain is not installed on this machine — `xcrun metal` exists but fails with "cannot execute tool 'metal'" (history #31, #33). I also cannot read the GPU's compiled pipeline state for register usage from the host API.
3) The one new attempt this round to get a cleaner occupancy figure — an NSLog of `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup` plus `maxThreadsPerSIMDGroup` at pipeline creation — never produced output: it failed to compile (the MTLDevice selector I used does not exist), and my follow-up isolated recompile to read the exact error also failed for an unrelated sandbox reason (`/tmp` not writable), so I have not re-run it (#249, #255).

Yes — the total-internal-reflection branch can fire, but only for rays that are *inside* the glass.

How I know it:

1. The Fresnel routine computes sin²θ_t = η²·(1 − cos²θ_i) and returns reflectance 1 when that exceeds 1. η is n_inside/n_outside at the interface being crossed.

2. Air→glass (rays hitting the bunny from outside — primary rays and the first hit on the outer surface): η = 1/1.5 = 2/3, so sin²θ_t ≤ (2/3)² = 4/9 < 1 for *every* incidence angle. TIR is mathematically impossible there; that branch is unreachable for outside rays.

3. Glass→air (rays already travelling inside the bunny, after the first refraction or after an internal reflection): η = 1.5, so sin²θ_t = 2.25·sin²θ_i > 1 once sin θ_i > 1/1.5, i.e. beyond the critical angle θ_c = asin(2/3) ≈ 41.81° from the surface normal (equivalently cos θ_i < √5/3 ≈ 0.745). Those rays reflectance = 1 and reflect instead of refracting.

So it fires on internal rays striking the inner wall at shallow grazing angles — a large fraction of them, which is exactly what traps light in the ears/legs and lets it leave in tight bundles to make the caustic.

Caveat on one round-5 result: the "TIR guard never fires" note in my log refers to the *guard I added* (skip Snell's law when reflectance ≥ 1) in the placement I tried, where the guard sat on the entering/outside path — unreachable for the reason in point 2. That is not a claim that the Fresnel function's own TIR branch is dead; it is live for the inside case. The experiment's bit-identical output is consistent with both readings, since when reflectance is 1 the BSDF branch reflects anyway.

Yes — it can trigger, but only in the direction where total internal reflection is physically impossible.

The guard is `sin2_t = (ior_t/ior_i)^2 * (1 - cos^2) > 1`, evaluated with `cos_incident = -dot(direction, oriented_normal)`, which is positive by construction, and with `ior_i = inside_glass ? 1.5 : 1.0`, `ior_t = inside_glass ? 1.0 : 1.5` (glass branch of pt_trace_path).

- Rays in air hitting the bunny (inside_glass == false): eta = 1.5/1 = 1.5, so sin2_t = 2.25 * sin^2(i). That exceeds 1 exactly when sin(i) > 2/3, i.e. incidence angle > asin(2/3) = 41.81 degrees. So the branch returns 1 for every outside ray that strikes the glass at grazing incidence — the bunny's silhouette/rim, the underside of the belly and feet, and generally the flanks of the lobes; these are common, not rare. Physically air->glass can never totally internally reflect, so this is a spurious TIR.
- Rays inside the glass leaving it (inside_glass == true): eta = 1/1.5 = 2/3, so sin2_t <= 4/9 < 1 for every angle, and the branch can NEVER fire — even though glass->air is precisely where real TIR occurs (theta > 41.81 degrees).

Why the render is still correct-ish: the code calls pt_refract with the opposite ratio (ior_i/ior_t = 1.5 inside the glass), and that function's own `sin2_t > 1` test is the physically correct one, so real TIR is caught there by `refracted == false`, and the branch `if (!refracted || pt_random(state) < reflectance)` reflects without consuming a random number. The two guards are complementary rather than consistent — that asymmetry is deliberate and frozen: it is exactly what the round-1 baseline rendered, so the reference caustic and the RMSE gates are defined by it (documented in the comment above pt_fresnel, [#14]).

One correction to my own notes: an earlier entry said the Fresnel guard "never fires" with ior 1.5. That is only true for the glass->air direction; for air->glass grazing rays it does fire, and that is why my round-5 "skip Snell when reflectance >= 1" micro-optimisation produced bit-identical images (when the guard fires, reflectance = 1 makes the draw always choose reflection, so the refract result was unused) — it was rejected purely on timing (base 43.315 ms min / 45.632 mean vs candidate 45.025 / 46.563 over 8 interleaved rounds, 6/8 favouring the base), not on correctness [#78].
